summary: This standards-track RFC specifies a way to provide active-active service at the TRILL edge, as described in RFC 7379, by letting end stations attach with multiple MAC addresses. This provides flow-level load balancing and resilience against link failure.

plainLanguage.summary: One computer can use several network addresses, each through a different door. If one door breaks, the others keep working.

subtitle: How TRILL edge switches share one group of hosts, and how remote switches learn to keep every attachment point instead of flip-flopping.

tldr.problem: When a host or bridge is connected to several RBridges at once, each RBridge ingresses its frames under its own nickname. A remote RBridge then sees the same MAC address arriving from different places and keeps changing its mind, which is called MAC address flip-flopping.
tldr.mechanism: Each member RBridge uses its own nickname as the ingress nickname. Remote RBridges keep all the attachments for a MAC address instead of replacing them. Under Option B, members announce those attachments through the ESADI protocol and remote RBridges stop learning those MAC addresses from decapsulated data frames.
tldr.outcome: Remote RBridges can send traffic to any member of the group and balance it per flow, without black-holes or triangular forwarding. If a remote RBridge supports neither option, the group must fall back to active-standby.

today: RFC 7782 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2016. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Active-Active Edge Problem
sections.content:
In a TRILL Active-Active Edge (AAE) topology, customer equipment such as a switch, virtual switch or multi-port end station is connected to several RBridges through a Local Active-Active Link Protocol (LAALP), for example a Multi-Chassis Link Aggregation (MC-LAG) bundle. Traffic in a VLAN can enter and leave through any of these RBridges at the same time, and end systems spread flows across the links. If a link fails, they keep using the remaining ones without waiting for TRILL to converge. The problem statement is in RFC 7379.

The catch is that a frame from one end node can be ingressed by any RBridge in the group. A remote edge RBridge may therefore see several egress RBridges for the same MAC address. This is MAC address flip-flopping.

This RFC solves it by letting the member RBridges use their own nicknames as ingress nicknames, and by requiring remote edge RBridges to keep several points of attachment per MAC address and Data Label (a VLAN or a Fine-Grained Label). The solution can run in one AAE group while another group in the same campus uses a different solution, such as the one in RFC 7781.
sections.plainLanguage: A kid can leave the house through any of several doors. The old way made the neighbors keep changing which door they thought the kid used. Now they just remember all the doors.

sections.title: Overview and Incremental Options
sections.content:
In the example topology, hosts H1 to H4 in VLAN 10 sit behind a bridge B that connects to RB1, RB2 and RB3 through LAALP1. RB4 is a remote RBridge outside the group. A member RBridge that conforms to this document always encapsulates a frame from its attached end nodes with its own nickname as the ingress nickname, whether the frame is unicast or multicast.

RB4 will therefore see multiple attachments per MAC address. Two options make that harmless.

  • Option A needs new hardware support: a capability announcement meaning that the RBridge can cope with data-plane learning of multiple attachments for an end node. Existing TRILL fast path hardware generally does not support it. The group can safely use this approach only if every interested edge RBridge announces the capability. Further details are out of scope, apart from a reserved capability bit.
  • Option B works with common existing fast path hardware, so it can be deployed incrementally. Member RBridges use the TRILL ESADI protocol to distribute the multiple attachments of a MAC address. Remote RBridges SHOULD disable data-plane MAC learning for such addresses, unless they also support Option A.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two ways to keep the address book right. One needs fancy new equipment. The other works with what people already have: the family sends a written note listing all their doors.

sections.title: How Option B Works
sections.content:
With Option B, a receiving edge RBridge MUST avoid flip-flop errors for MAC addresses learned from decapsulated TRILL Data packets. It is RECOMMENDED that it disable data-plane learning in the advertised Data Labels for the originating RBridge. An alternative that gives the same behavior is acceptable. For example, the receiver can use the confidence-level mechanism from RFC 6325, giving a value such as 0x21 to the first attachment learned from the data plane and a higher value such as 0x80 to attachments learned from ESADI so that ESADI overrides them.

An RBridge in an AAE group MUST participate in ESADI in the Data Labels enabled for its LAALPs. Two new flags, both named AA, are allocated from the Interested VLANs and Interested Labels flag bits. When set to 1, they say that the Data Labels are advertised for LAALPs rather than plain LAN links.

Remote edge RBridges discover the group members by listening for the AA-LAALP-GROUP-RBRIDGES APPsub-TLV, carried in the TRILL GENINFO TLV in FS-LSPs. It holds the sender nickname that the member will use as its ingress nickname, and the LAALP ID. For an MC-LAG or DRNI the ID is the 8-byte ID from Clause 6.3.2 of 802.1AX. It rarely changes, only when a group is created or removed or a link to the CE fails or recovers.

Whenever MAC addresses are learned from the LAALP, through ingress or configuration, the member MUST advertise them in a MAC-Reachability TLV via ESADI, wrapped in the AA-LAALP-GROUP-MAC APPsub-TLV. Its confidence value SHOULD be set to prevail over addresses learned from decapsulation. A remote RBridge sends traffic for those addresses to the closest group member by least cost, and picks pseudorandomly among equal-cost members. Other members of the same group SHOULD learn the addresses as if the end nodes were locally attached.
sections.plainLanguage: Each door keeper sends a note saying which kids live behind their door. Everyone else reads the notes and sends mail to the nearest door that has the kid.

sections.title: Meeting the Design Goals
sections.content:
The RFC walks through the goals of an active-active edge.

  • No flip-flopping. Because remote RBridges see all attachments in ESADI, one learned from a member is not overwritten by another. For return traffic the remote RBridge consistently uses one attachment per MAC address.
  • Regular ingress. The LAALP delivers each frame to the group over exactly one uplink, so each member just ingresses it per RFC 6325, assuming it is the Appointed Forwarder for the VLANs on that uplink.
  • No duplication. For multi-destination packets from the campus, exactly one member must egress each packet. The members use the LAALP's own selection function (hashing or an election algorithm). The selected RBridge MUST egress the packet and the others MUST NOT.
  • No echo. A multi-destination frame ingressed by one member must not be sent back into the LAALP by another. Members use split horizon with a per-port filter list of <ingress nickname, VLAN> tuples, built from the group-membership APPsub-TLVs. In Figure 1, RB3 filters {<RB1, VLAN 10>, <RB2, VLAN 10>} on its LAALP port.
  • No black-hole or triangular forwarding. When a sub-link fails, the affected member uses ESADI to flush the affected MAC addresses, so remote RBridges stop sending toward the failed port and the member does not need to redirect packets to its peers.
  • Load balance. A remote RBridge can spread traffic per flow across the members, not just along the least-cost path. This does not replace the LAALP's own load balancing; the two work separately.
sections.plainLanguage: The group has rules so that only one door keeper hands over each shared message, nobody passes a kid's own message back to them, and if a door breaks everyone is told right away.

sections.title: Capability Flags, Scalability and Compatibility
sections.content:
The EXTENDED-RBRIDGE-CAP APPsub-TLV (type 254, length 10) goes in E-L1FS FS-LSP fragment zero. Its capability bits are E (bit 0, the RBridge acts as Option B) and H (bit 1, it keeps multiple attachments learned from decapsulation in fast path hardware, which is Option A). Bits 2 through 63 are reserved: they MUST be sent as zero and ignored on receipt.

If a member RBridge sees a remote RBridge interested in the group's Data Labels that supports neither Option A nor Option B, the AAE group MUST fall back to active-standby mode.

On scalability, Option A uses extra MAC table entries, which usually fit in unused table space because LAALP-attached addresses are a small part of the campus. With Option B, the multiple attachments live in the ESADI link-state databases, normally kept in software, while the hardware MAC table still holds one entry per MAC address.

The new TLVs travel in Extended Level 1 Flooding Scope (E-L1FS) PDUs. An RBridge that does not support E-L1FS will not send the capability TLV, and MAC multi-attach active-active is not supported with it.
sections.plainLanguage: Each switch holds up a small card saying which trick it knows. If someone in the room knows neither trick, the family goes back to using one door at a time.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Extensions carried by ESADI follow the security considerations of RFC 7357. Extensions not carried by ESADI can be protected by configuring RBridges to include the IS-IS Authentication TLV (10) in IS-IS PDUs, using IS-IS security from RFC 5304 and RFC 5310.

The LAALPs deployed at the time are proprietary, so security over membership in and internal management of AAE groups is proprietary too. Without authentication, a rogue RBridge that insinuates itself into a group can disrupt end-station traffic in or out of it. With N RBridges in the group, it could typically control 1/Nth of the traffic flowing out of the group and a similar amount of unicast traffic flowing in.
sections.plainLanguage: If a stranger sneaks into the group of door keepers, they can grab their share of the mail. Passwords between the switches keep strangers out.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA allocated three types in the TRILL APPsub-TLV registry under IS-IS TLV 251, Application Identifier 1: 252 AA-LAALP-GROUP-RBRIDGES, 253 AA-LAALP-GROUP-MAC and 254 EXTENDED-RBRIDGE-CAP.

IANA also created an Extended RBridge Capabilities registry with Expert Review: bit 0 is E (Option B support), bit 1 is H (Option A support), and bits 2 to 63 are unassigned. Two AA flag bits were allocated, bit 16 from the Interested VLANs Flag Bits and bit 4 from the Interested Labels Flag Bits.
sections.plainLanguage: The numbers and flags this RFC uses were written into the official list so nobody else uses them for something different.

fields.desc: Nickname the originating RBridge will use as ingress nickname.

fields.desc: Length k of the LAALP ID in bytes.

fields.desc: The LAALP ID, k bytes long (variable).

fields.name: Topology
fields.desc: Topology the capabilities apply to; zero means all or none in use.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Bits 2 onward, sent as zero and ignored on receipt.
